challenge.exploration_summary: The helmet project is a Node.js security middleware library for Express/Connect. It consists of independent middleware modules (content-security-policy, strict-transport-security, x-frame-options, etc.) that set HTTP security headers. The content-security-policy module is the most feature-rich middleware, supporting directive-based configuration, function-based directive values for dynamic policies, and report-only mode. The project has excellent test coverage (124 tests, all passing) using Node's built-in test runner with supertest for integration tests.
challenge.feature_spec: Added two new helper functions to the content-security-policy middleware: createNonce() and getNonce(res). createNonce() returns a ContentSecurityPolicyDirectiveValueFunction that generates a cryptographically random 16-byte nonce per response, stores it in a WeakMap keyed by the ServerResponse object, and returns the properly quoted CSP directive value (e.g., 'nonce-abc123...'). The nonce is reused if called multiple times on the same response. getNonce(res) retrieves the raw nonce from a response object, allowing application code (e.g., template engines) to include the nonce in <script> or <style> tags. Both functions are exported from the module and from the main helmet index.
challenge.feature_rationale: CSP nonces are a widely used mechanism to allow inline scripts/styles without resorting to 'unsafe-inline'. They require the same random value to appear in both the CSP header and the HTML tags. The existing CSP middleware already supports function-based directive values that receive (req, res), making this the natural place to add nonce support. By storing the nonce on the response via a WeakMap and providing a getter, users can easily retrieve the nonce in their templates without manual bookkeeping. This avoids memory leaks (WeakMap) and follows the existing patterns of the codebase.
challenge.bug_description: The getNonce(res) function destructively deletes the nonce from the WeakMap after retrieving it. This means that calling getNonce() multiple times on the same response object returns the nonce only on the first call and undefined on subsequent calls. Since getNonce is documented as a pure getter, application code (e.g., template engines) that retrieves the nonce more than once for the same response will silently receive undefined after the first call, causing the nonce to be missing from some script/style tags and breaking CSP nonce enforcement.

findings.description: The ContentSecurityPolicy interface definition was corrupted by a bad merge. The createNonce and getNonce property declarations were placed inside the interface body between the call signature and its remaining properties, and the function implementations (nonceStore, createNonce(), getNonce()) were erroneously inserted inside the interface block as well. This causes TypeScript compilation to fail with multiple syntax errors (TS1005, TS1359, TS1390, TS1109, TS1128). The interface is missing the closing of the call signature return type (next parameter).

getNonce() deletes the nonce from the WeakMap after retrieving it (nonceStore.delete(res)). This breaks the use case where application code needs to retrieve the same nonce multiple times — for example, inserting it into both a <script> tag and a <style> tag. The second call to getNonce() returns undefined, causing a broken page. The WeakMap already handles cleanup automatically when the ServerResponse object is garbage collected, so manual deletion is unnecessary and harmful.

self_review.fix_explanation: Two issues were fixed: (1) The ContentSecurityPolicy interface was rewritten to have the correct structure — the createNonce and getNonce property type declarations are now properly placed inside the interface alongside getDefaultDirectives and dangerouslyDisableDefaultSrc, while the actual function implementations (nonceStore, createNonce(), getNonce()) are placed outside the interface, after the dangerouslyDisableDefaultSrc symbol definition. (2) The nonceStore.delete(res) call was removed from getNonce(), so it now simply returns nonceStore.get(res) without destroying the stored nonce. This allows application code to call getNonce() multiple times on the same response (e.g., for multiple script/style tags) and always get the same nonce value.
